key: E♭ major (written score; playback pitch unverified)
performers: Marian Anderson, contralto; San Francisco Symphony Orchestra; Pierre Monteux, conductor
intro: Marian Anderson sings the fourth of the Kindertotenlieder, “Oft denk’ ich, sie sind nur ausgegangen”, with Pierre Monteux and the San Francisco Symphony. A parent repeats that the children will soon be home, harp and cellos play a walking figure beneath the tune, and the final stanza says the children have gone ahead for good.

sections.label: A · The children’s long walk
sections.mNote: Horn, violins and moving cellos introduce the song

sections.label: A′ · The promise repeated
sections.mNote: Clarinets and bassoon surround the contralto

sections.label: A″ · Last stanza, harp and cellos
sections.mNote: Harp and cellos accompany the last stanza.

cues.title: Horn and violins over walking bass
cues.text: Harp and plucked double bass play a steady walking bass beneath the horn and violins. The cellos have a quicker, winding figure of their own. In Anderson’s first stanza the children are imagined taking a long walk on a beautiful day.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460 (1905), pp. 48–49: opening instrumentation and Rückert’s first stanza. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Second stanza, “O sei nicht bang”
cues.text: “O sei nicht bang” means “oh, do not be afraid”. Rückert repeats the reassurance, rearranging the same few words. Anderson sings the returning tune with clarinets and bassoon close beside her, and the strings play less around the voice.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, p. 52 onwards, second stanza; our translation of Rückert’s words. The established section marks the stanza’s opening.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Separate printing, 10 May 1905
cues.text: On 10 May 1905 this song, alone of the five, was printed separately in a version for voice and piano, as the music supplement to the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik. Mahler had stipulated that the cycle be kept together. The periodical’s publisher, Kahnt, issued the complete cycle later that year.
cues.evidence: Mahler catalogue, Kindertotenlieder: chronology (10 May 1905) and the description of the supplement to Neue Zeitschrift für Musik 72/20, published by Kahnt, “despite Mahler’s stipulation that the cycle was to be considered an indivisible whole”: https://www.mahlercat.org.uk/Pages/KtL/KtLprints.htm

cues.title: Last stanza, rehearsal 5
cues.text: The last stanza sets the line “Sie sind uns nur vorausgegangen” (they have only gone ahead of us). Anderson sings it to the same melody. The harp plays underneath, and the cellos continue their short figures.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, p. 56, rehearsal 5; Rückert’s last stanza, our translation. Harmonic names in the score refer to its printed pitch; the transfer’s playback pitch remains unverified.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Postlude, horn and bassoon
cues.text: The poem’s sunny heights take the voice upwards before the short instrumental ending. After Anderson stops, horn and bassoon continue, with harp and soft strings. The last chord is marked “morendo” — dying away.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, p. 59, final phrase and postlude. The existing closing cue locates this passage; our translation of morendo.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Clarinets take over at a tempo
transitions.how: A poco ritardando slows the end of the first stanza. At the return to a tempo the harp and most of the strings stop. Clarinets play the moving line over bassoon notes as Anderson sings “Ja wohl” again.

transitions.title: Harp and cellos return for last stanza
transitions.to: A″ · Last stanza, harp and cellos
transitions.how: The harp’s repeated notes return with the bowed cello figure, and clarinets play above as the voice begins the last stanza, marked schlicht (plain). Mahler restores the tempo but adds Nicht eilen.

source.title: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, full score (C. F. Kahnt, plate 4460)
source.locator: Song IV, printed pp. 48–59: horn, violins and moving cellos at the opening, clarinets at the second stanza and the quiet orchestral close.

timeline.note: Horn and violins share the tune above moving cellos, harp and plucked double basses.
Anderson takes up the opening tune as the father imagines the children coming home.
Clarinets answer the singer above a bassoon line at the start of the second stanza.
Running cellos and the harp’s repeated notes accompany the last stanza.

composer.epithet: Conductor who composed during the summers and intended each symphony to contain a whole world, combining the sublime with the music of the street band.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. In Iglau he heard bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church, and these sounds recur throughout his music. Late in life he told Sigmund Freud that he had once run from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was playing Ach, du lieber Augustin.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, where he studied piano and composition, and he sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. Among his friends were Hugo Wolf and Hans Rott, who died young. Rott’s symphony is so close to Mahler’s own music that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. By then he had already begun his career as a conductor, and that career would pay for everything else.
